bull_bear.body: Defence budget allocations; Competition from global players
bull_bear.title: Risks & watch-items

bull_bear.body: The company's credit rating revision reflects its stable financial performance and outlook, but the company faces risks related to defence budget allocations and competition from global players.
bull_bear.title: Non-obvious takeaways

bull_bear.body:
- Long-standing relationships with global defence and aerospace OEMs, including authorisation since 2018 to export munitions list items to IAI ELTA Systems, Israel
- Integrated capabilities spanning cable and wire harness, PCBA, system integration, testing and qualification
- Backward integration through wholly owned subsidiary Raneal Advanced Systems into high-reliability PCBA/EMS, improving control over quality, sourcing and delivery
- Consolidated order book of approximately ₹2,984 crore as at March 31, 2026, providing medium-term execution visibility
- Location inside the Hi-Tech Defence and Aerospace Park SEZ, Bengaluru, supporting customer proximity and export/deemed-export supply
- High qualification barriers to entry in defence electronics — customer approvals, traceability, testing and programme continuity act as important barriers
- Technology-transfer and localisation pathways through the ELTX Systems and NIART Systems joint ventures with ELTA Systems (Israel)
- Approved Indian Offset Partner status with the Ministry of Defence, with growing participation in non-offset programmes
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Programme execution and milestone risk — Delays in qualification, certification, customer approvals or milestone completion can defer revenue recognition. This is not theoretical: FY 2025-26 revenue moderated materially because of extended qualification and certification timelines across certain defence programmes, and the Board itself attributes the decline to the timing of project milestones, deferred order execution and the nature of long-gestation defence programmes. Mitigated through programme-level monitoring, customer coordination, defined execution milestones and periodic management review.
- Supply-chain and imported-component dependence, including export-licence delays — Dependence on specialised and imported components exposes operations to shortages, export-licence delays and geopolitical disruptions; the SWOT lists exposure to specialised imported components as a weakness, and FY26 execution was hit by supply-chain disruptions, delays in export licences for critical components and restricted movement of materials and technical personnel. Mitigated through an approved vendor framework, alternate-source development, procurement planning, inventory buffers for critical components and traceability controls.
- Working-capital intensity and liquidity risk — Defence programmes involve extended procurement and execution cycles, and the SWOT flags working-capital intensity associated with high-value components and longer qualification periods as a structural weakness. Mitigated through budgeting, cash-flow monitoring, working-capital planning, receivables review and conservative balance-sheet management.
- Technology and obsolescence risk — Rapid changes in radar, electronic warfare and defence electronics can affect product relevance and component availability, and rapid technology evolution and obsolescence risk is named as a threat in the SWOT. Mitigated through Transfer of Technology arrangements, strategic partnerships, obsolescence management, capability upgrades and continued participation in new programme opportunities.
- Regulatory, industrial-licensing and export-control risk — Defence manufacturing is subject to industrial licensing, security classifications, export controls and customer-country regulations; regulatory, qualification and programme delays are listed as a threat. Mitigated through legal and secretarial review, compliance monitoring, licence tracking, export documentation controls and periodic statutory reviews.
- Cybersecurity, data-security and intellectual-property risk — Defence programmes involve sensitive military and aviation-related technical and customer information, so a breach of information systems can cause operational disruption, financial loss, reputational damage and regulatory or legal consequences. The BRSR names Data Security Risk as a material issue. Mitigated through access controls, licensed systems, information-security procedures, routine security audits, vulnerability assessments, employee training and restricted access to sensitive information.
- Quality and compliance risk in a mission-critical industry — Failure to meet defence, aerospace or customer-specific standards can affect qualification and programme continuity, and customer approvals and traceability act as high barriers that cut both ways. Mitigated through AS9100:2016, ISO 9001:2015, IPC standards, controlled manufacturing processes, inspection, testing and documented quality systems.
- Customer, geographic and export concentration — The Company operates as a single business segment with 100% of turnover from the manufacture of defence and aerospace related products, and exports contribute 58.04% of total turnover including deemed exports (BRSR Section A, read from the registry/governance bundles of the same annual report). Revenue depends on customer schedules, approvals and programme milestones, and the SWOT names this dependence explicitly, leaving the business exposed to a narrow set of OEM relationships and to Israel/US-centred defence demand.
- Human-capital and specialist-skill risk — Specialist technical skills are critical to execution quality and continuity in high-reliability defence manufacturing, and the workforce is small — 89 permanent employees and 139 workers as at March 31, 2026. Mitigated through structured recruitment, training, skill development, performance reviews, succession planning and employee-welfare practices.
- Materials sourcing and critical-input availability — The BRSR identifies materials sourcing and efficiency as a material risk: aerospace and defence manufacturing depends on critical raw materials with few substitutes sourced from a small number of countries, so supply-chain disruption, geopolitical uncertainty and rising global demand can affect availability, price volatility and production continuity. Mitigated through proactive procurement, qualified supplier management, alternative sourcing evaluation and inventory levels for key materials.
- Subsidiary development-stage losses and unproven commercialisation — Consolidated profitability turned negative in FY 2025-26 principally because NIART Systems Limited remained in the product-development and R&D phase and had not commenced commercial production; Form AOC-1 lists both NIART Systems Ltd and ELTX Systems Private Limited as yet to commence operations, so a substantial share of deployed capital is still pre-revenue and dependent on trials, qualification and technology transfer succeeding.
- Business continuity risk — Fire, natural events, IT disruption or facility interruption can affect programme delivery from a footprint concentrated in Bengaluru. Mitigated through insurance cover, fire and safety systems, emergency procedures, drills, data backup and continuity planning.

business.body: Aerospace and defence manufacturing; Details not disclosed
business.title: Segment / subsidiary detail

business.body: Established in 2011, DCX manufactures complex cable and wire harness assemblies and has expanded across the defence value chain into RF and microwave transmit-receivers, missile switching units, mission control systems, antenna assemblies, radar processor units, electronic subsystems and radar-related systems, alongside system integration, testing and qualification. It serves global original equipment manufacturers, system integrators and Indian defence entities across land, naval and airborne applications. Through wholly owned subsidiary Raneal Advanced Systems it is backward-integrated into high-reliability PCBA/EMS, and it participates in radar, electronic warfare and railway obstacle-detection programmes through joint ventures with ELTA Systems (Israel).
business.title: What they do

business.body:
- **System Integration Assemblies:** RF and microwave transmit-receiver groups, Missile switching modules, Mission control systems, Antenna assemblies, Radar processor units, Digital transmit-receive and digital receiver modules for high-power radars, Air defence fire control radar systems, Air defence and ground-based radar systems, Airborne radar systems
- **Cable and Wire Harness:** Wire harnesses for radar, missile, communication and electronic warfare applications
- **Kitting:** Kitting
- **High-reliability electronics (Raneal Advanced Systems):** High-reliability printed circuit board assemblies (PCBA), Circuit card assemblies
- **Joint-venture platforms:** SEE FAR railway obstacle-detection radar and optronics (NIART Systems), Advanced Tank Counter-UAS Self-Protection Solution (with IAI ELTA)
business.title: Products & brands

business.body:
- Raneal Advanced Systems Private Limited — subsidiary: 100% wholly owned subsidiary; backward integration into EMS / PCBA; commenced commercial production in 2023 and secured an industrial licence in 2024; operates the dedicated ISO 8 / Class 100k clean-room PCBA facility
- NIART Systems Ltd, Israel — subsidiary: 100% wholly owned subsidiary incorporated in Israel with a JV relationship with ELTA Systems (Israel); develops railway obstacle-detection radar and optics solutions (SEE FAR); reporting period 01.01.2025 to 31.12.2025, reported in NIS; listed in Form AOC-1 as yet to commence operations
- ELTX Systems Private Limited — associate: Associate / joint venture with ELTA Systems Ltd (Israel) for radar and electronic warfare systems for airborne and land applications; DCX holds 92,500 equity shares of ₹10 each, extent of holding 37%, with significant influence by way of 37% voting power under the Joint Venture Agreement; associated/acquired on October 10, 2025; listed as yet to commence operations

outlook.body: Stable outlook; Focus on defence modernization and aerospace manufacturing
outlook.title: Guidance / outlook

outlook.body: Growing order book; Details not disclosed
outlook.title: Order book & pipeline

outlook.body:
- Strengthen the core: expand cable and wire harness assemblies and established manufacturing competencies across radar, missile, communication, UAV and electronic warfare applications.
- Backward integration through Raneal Advanced Systems Private Limited to expand high-reliability PCBA capability and supply-chain control, serving both captive requirements and external customer programmes.
- Move up from component-level manufacturing to greater system responsibility — deeper participation across electronic subsystems, radar-related integration, testing and qualification.
- Diversify the programme mix by increasing non-offset participation while retaining established offset capabilities, reducing dependence on any single procurement model.
- Progress technology-led products through the ELTX Systems and NIART Systems joint ventures with ELTA Systems (Israel), creating pathways for technology transfer, localisation and commercialisation.
- Enter new markets and geographies — engaging global OEMs, expanding export-led opportunities and selectively entering adjacent high-reliability sectors.
- Maintain financial flexibility to fund longer programme cycles and working-capital requirements while investing in product development, R&D and technology-led capability creation.
- Advance the ELTX Systems platform through the Tamil Nadu radar and electronic warfare manufacturing facility initiative under Make in India.
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: DCX's expansion is footprint- and capability-led rather than quantified in rupee terms. The Company operates from the Hi-Tech Defence and Aerospace Park SEZ at Devanahalli, Bengaluru, where it commissioned a new manufacturing facility in 2020 after signing a lease for 6,070 sq m of land in the Aerospace SEZ in 2018; BRSR Section A reports two national plants and two national offices across three states, with the corporate office inside the Bengaluru SEZ unit and an additional plant/office in the Domestic Tariff Area at Defence and Aerospace Park, Bengaluru. Backward integration runs through wholly owned subsidiary Raneal Advanced Systems Private Limited, which commenced commercial production in 2023, established a circuit card assembly facility with IPC Class 3 capabilities and an ISO 8 / Class 100k clean room, secured an industrial licence in 2024, and during FY 2025-26 expanded its manufacturing capability through an oversized PCBA facility alongside increased participation in surveillance and electronic warfare opportunities. On the joint-venture side, DCX signed a Memorandum of Understanding with the Government of Tamil Nadu through its nodal agency Guidance at the 'TN Rising Investment Conclave' in Hosur, facilitating the setup of a state-of-the-art radar manufacturing facility for the ELTX Systems joint venture with ELTA Systems Ltd, Israel, strengthening the Tamil Nadu Defence Industrial Corridor; the MD&A records that the ELTX platform was advanced through this Tamil Nadu manufacturing facility initiative for radar and electronic warfare systems under Make in India. NIART Systems remained in the product-development and R&D phase during FY26, progressing its SEE FAR railway obstacle-detection programme through functional and fog trials with RDSO and subsequent prototype deployment and accumulation runs, without commencing commercial production. Capital raised for this next phase came from a ₹5,000 Mn qualified institutions placement completed in January 2024, of which ₹2,090 Mn had been invested in NIART Systems Limited and ₹2,778 Mn of unutilised proceeds remained in bank fixed deposits available for deployment in accordance with the stated objects of the QIP. During FY26 the Company also obtained a Defence Industrial Licence covering radar systems, electronic warfare systems, avionics and other defence electronic equipment under Category-A classification, and its capability set expanded to include airborne radar systems. NOTE ON SOURCING: the Tamil Nadu MoU, the Raneal oversized PCBA expansion, the Defence Industrial Licence, the QIP capital bridge and the 6,070 sq m SEZ lease were read from the Corporate Overview, Chairman/MD Message and MD&A sections routed into the profile and strategy_outlook bundles of this same annual report; the capex_expansion bundle's own MD&A extract was truncated to the Directors'-Report tail and did not carry the operational review.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- Sustained defence modernisation and security-led government expenditure: global military expenditure rose 2.9% in real terms in 2025, an eleventh consecutive annual rise, with India the fifth-largest military spender at $92.1 billion.
- Indian defence indigenisation: defence production reached a record ₹1.78 lakh crore in FY 2025-26, up 15.6%, with private-sector participation at 24% of production and exports of ₹38,424 crore, up 62.66% year on year.
- Domestic procurement allocation: 75% of the FY 2025-26 modernisation budget (₹1,11,544.83 crore) was earmarked for domestic sources, with ₹27,886.21 crore provisioned for procurement through domestic private industry; the FY 2026-27 defence budget further reinforces domestic manufacturing with approximately 75% of the capital acquisition allocation.
- Policy support through Aatmanirbhar Bharat, Defence Acquisition Procedure 2020, Positive Indigenisation Lists and Transfer of Technology arrangements encouraging local manufacturing and system integration.
- Rising demand for high-reliability assemblies, RF and microwave electronics, radar subsystems, secure communication architectures and system-level integration as defence platforms become more electronics-intensive.
- High qualification thresholds — customer approvals, traceability, testing and programme continuity — act as important barriers to entry for defence electronics manufacturers.
- FY26 revenue moderation was attributed to supply-chain disruptions, delays in export licences for critical components, restricted movement of materials and technical personnel, and extended qualification and certification timelines.
- Management has indicated easing supply-chain conditions, greater predictability in export-licence processes and continued progression of key programmes through qualification milestones going into FY 2026-27.
- Consolidated profitability is being weighed down by NIART Systems, which remained in the product-development and R&D stage and had not commenced commercial production during FY26.
- Directors expect strategic engagement with existing and prospective customers and participation in indigenous defence programmes to support long-term growth and improve the order pipeline in coming years.
- Consolidated closing order book of approximately ₹2,984 crore as at March 31, 2026, compared with ₹2,855 crore a year earlier, supported by continued domestic and international order inflows.
- The order book is described as providing medium-term revenue/execution visibility as programme execution normalises, and DCX enters FY 2026-27 with it in place.
- Secured a major order of approximately ₹563 crore for the manufacture and supply of a Maritime Patrol Radar System for airborne application during FY 2025-26.
- Secured an order of approximately ₹68 crore from Hindustan Aeronautics Limited for antennas and power supplies during FY 2025-26.
outlook.title: Demand & outlook drivers

deepdive.thesis: DCX Systems Limited is a leading player in the aerospace and defence sector, with a strong manufacturing presence and a growing order book. The company's credit rating has been revised to Crisil BBB+/Stable, reflecting its stable financial performance and outlook. However, the company faces risks related to defence budget allocations and competition from global players.

The Company operates from the Hi-Tech Defence and Aerospace Park SEZ at Devanahalli, Bengaluru, where it commissioned a new manufacturing facility in 2020 after signing a lease for 6,070 sq m of land in the Aerospace SEZ in 2018; BRSR Section A reports two national plants and two national offices across three states, with the corporate office inside the Bengaluru SEZ unit and an additional plant/office in the Domestic Tariff Area at Defence and Aerospace Park, Bengaluru. On the joint-venture side, DCX signed a Memorandum of Understanding with the Government of Tamil Nadu through its nodal agency Guidance at the 'TN Rising Investment Conclave' in Hosur, facilitating the setup of a state-of-the-art radar manufacturing facility for the ELTX Systems joint venture with ELTA Systems Ltd, Israel, strengthening the Tamil Nadu Defence Industrial Corridor; the MD&A records that the ELTX platform was advanced through this Tamil Nadu manufacturing facility initiative for radar and electronic warfare systems under Make in India. NIART Systems remained in the product-development and R&D phase during FY26, progressing its SEE FAR railway obstacle-detection programme through functional and fog trials with RDSO and subsequent prototype deployment and accumulation runs, without commencing commercial production. Capital raised for this next phase came from a ₹5,000 Mn qualified institutions placement completed in January 2024, of which ₹2,090 Mn had been invested in NIART Systems Limited and ₹2,778 Mn of unutilised proceeds remained in bank fixed deposits available for deployment in accordance with the stated objects of the QIP. During FY26 the Company also obtained a Defence Industrial Licence covering radar systems, electronic warfare systems, avionics and other defence electronic equipment under Category-A classification, and its capability set expanded to include airborne radar systems. risks.note: Delays in qualification, certification, customer approvals or milestone completion can defer revenue recognition. This is not theoretical: FY 2025-26 revenue moderated materially because of extended qualification and certification timelines across certain defence programmes, and the Board itself attributes the decline to the timing of project milestones, deferred order execution and the nature of long-gestation defence programmes. Mitigated through programme-level monitoring, customer coordination, defined execution milestones and periodic management review.

risks.risk: Supply-chain and imported-component dependence, including export-licence delays
risks.note: Dependence on specialised and imported components exposes operations to shortages, export-licence delays and geopolitical disruptions; the SWOT lists exposure to specialised imported components as a weakness, and FY26 execution was hit by supply-chain disruptions, delays in export licences for critical components and restricted movement of materials and technical personnel. Mitigated through an approved vendor framework, alternate-source development, procurement planning, inventory buffers for critical components and traceability controls.

Defence programmes involve extended procurement and execution cycles, and the SWOT flags working-capital intensity associated with high-value components and longer qualification periods as a structural weakness. Mitigated through budgeting, cash-flow monitoring, working-capital planning, receivables review and conservative balance-sheet management.

Rapid changes in radar, electronic warfare and defence electronics can affect product relevance and component availability, and rapid technology evolution and obsolescence risk is named as a threat in the SWOT. Mitigated through Transfer of Technology arrangements, strategic partnerships, obsolescence management, capability upgrades and continued participation in new programme opportunities.

Defence manufacturing is subject to industrial licensing, security classifications, export controls and customer-country regulations; regulatory, qualification and programme delays are listed as a threat. Mitigated through legal and secretarial review, compliance monitoring, licence tracking, export documentation controls and periodic statutory reviews.

Defence programmes involve sensitive military and aviation-related technical and customer information, so a breach of information systems can cause operational disruption, financial loss, reputational damage and regulatory or legal consequences. The BRSR names Data Security Risk as a material issue. Mitigated through access controls, licensed systems, information-security procedures, routine security audits, vulnerability assessments, employee training and restricted access to sensitive information.

risks.risk: Quality and compliance risk in a mission-critical industry
risks.note: Failure to meet defence, aerospace or customer-specific standards can affect qualification and programme continuity, and customer approvals and traceability act as high barriers that cut both ways. Mitigated through AS9100:2016, ISO 9001:2015, IPC standards, controlled manufacturing processes, inspection, testing and documented quality systems.

The Company operates as a single business segment with 100% of turnover from the manufacture of defence and aerospace related products, and exports contribute 58.04% of total turnover including deemed exports (BRSR Section A, read from the registry/governance bundles of the same annual report). Revenue depends on customer schedules, approvals and programme milestones, and the SWOT names this dependence explicitly, leaving the business exposed to a narrow set of OEM relationships and to Israel/US-centred defence demand.

Specialist technical skills are critical to execution quality and continuity in high-reliability defence manufacturing, and the workforce is small — 89 permanent employees and 139 workers as at March 31, 2026. Mitigated through structured recruitment, training, skill development, performance reviews, succession planning and employee-welfare practices.

The BRSR identifies materials sourcing and efficiency as a material risk: aerospace and defence manufacturing depends on critical raw materials with few substitutes sourced from a small number of countries, so supply-chain disruption, geopolitical uncertainty and rising global demand can affect availability, price volatility and production continuity. Mitigated through proactive procurement, qualified supplier management, alternative sourcing evaluation and inventory levels for key materials.

risks.risk: Subsidiary development-stage losses and unproven commercialisation
risks.note: Consolidated profitability turned negative in FY 2025-26 principally because NIART Systems Limited remained in the product-development and R&D phase and had not commenced commercial production; Form AOC-1 lists both NIART Systems Ltd and ELTX Systems Private Limited as yet to commence operations, so a substantial share of deployed capital is still pre-revenue and dependent on trials, qualification and technology transfer succeeding.

Fire, natural events, IT disruption or facility interruption can affect programme delivery from a footprint concentrated in Bengaluru. Mitigated through insurance cover, fire and safety systems, emergency procedures, drills, data backup and continuity planning.

one-line thesis: DCX Systems Limited is a leading player in the aerospace and defence sector, with a strong manufacturing presence and a growing order book. The company's credit rating has been revised to Crisil BBB+/Stable, reflecting its stable financial performance and outlook. However, the company faces risks related to defence budget allocations and competition from global players.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Sustained defence modernisation and security-led government expenditure: global military expenditure rose 2.9% in real terms in 2025, an eleventh consecutive annual rise, with India the fifth-largest military spender at $92.1 billion.

- Policy support through Aatmanirbhar Bharat, Defence Acquisition Procedure 2020, Positive Indigenisation Lists and Transfer of Technology arrangements encouraging local manufacturing and system integration.
- Rising demand for high-reliability assemblies, RF and microwave electronics, radar subsystems, secure communication architectures and system-level integration as defence platforms become more electronics-intensive.
- High qualification thresholds — customer approvals, traceability, testing and programme continuity — act as important barriers to entry for defence electronics manufacturers.
- FY26 revenue moderation was attributed to supply-chain disruptions, delays in export licences for critical components, restricted movement of materials and technical personnel, and extended qualification and certification timelines.

- Directors expect strategic engagement with existing and prospective customers and participation in indigenous defence programmes to support long-term growth and improve the order pipeline in coming years.
- Consolidated closing order book of approximately ₹2,984 crore as at March 31, 2026, compared with ₹2,855 crore a year earlier, supported by continued domestic and international order inflows.
- The order book is described as providing medium-term revenue/execution visibility as programme execution normalises, and DCX enters FY 2026-27 with it in place.
- Secured a major order of approximately ₹563 crore for the manufacture and supply of a Maritime Patrol Radar System for airborne application during FY 2025-26.
- Secured an order of approximately ₹68 crore from Hindustan Aeronautics Limited for antennas and power supplies during FY 2025-26.
